title: Aussie Oddities
blurb: Big things, odd inventions and true stories from the wide brown land.

prompts.text: In 1932, soldiers with machine guns were sent into the WA wheatbelt to fight an invasion of _____. They lost.
Vegemite was first developed in 1922 by the Melbourne chemist _____.
The Hills Hoist rotary clothesline was first built in a backyard in _____.
The Big Banana, one of Australia's best-known big things, stands in _____.
The world's first feature-length film, made in Australia in 1906, told the story of _____.
The aircraft flight recorder, or black box, was invented by the Australian scientist _____.
A key patent behind modern Wi-Fi came from Australia's national science agency, the _____.
Australian _____ shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for turning penicillin into a usable medicine.
The multi-channel cochlear implant, or bionic ear, was pioneered by Australian surgeon _____.
The lamington is named after Lord Lamington, a former Governor of _____.
Lake Hillier, on an island off Western Australia's south coast, is naturally _____.
Canberra was designed by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and _____.
In the outback town of Coober Pedy, many locals escape the heat by living in underground homes called _____.
After Prime Minister Harold Holt vanished at sea in 1967, a Melbourne _____ was named in his memory.
Before it was renamed Tasmania, the island was officially called _____.
Australia's official national gemstone is the _____.
Frank Forde is Australia's shortest-serving Prime Minister, in office for just _____ days.
Long before he was Prime Minister, Bob Hawke set a record at Oxford for drinking a yard of _____ at speed.
Melbourne has the largest urban _____ network in the world.
Rottnest Island got its name because a Dutch explorer mistook the quokkas for giant _____.
Western Australia's Wave Rock sits just outside the small wheatbelt town of _____.
The thorny devil can drink through its _____, which channels water up to its mouth.
The Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor includes Australia's longest dead-straight road, nicknamed the _____.
The Sydney Opera House was designed by the Danish architect Jørn _____.
A giant concrete sheep called the Big Merino stands in the NSW city of _____.
Edwin Flack, Australia's first Olympic champion, won his two gold medals in 1896 at the Games in _____.
Cyclone _____ flattened much of Darwin on Christmas Day 1974.
Don Bradman needed just _____ runs in his final Test innings to finish with an average of 100.
Tim Tams were named after a racehorse that won the 1958 Kentucky _____.
The Royal Flying Doctor Service was founded in 1928 by the Reverend _____.
The superb lyrebird is such a good mimic that it has been recorded copying camera shutters and _____.
Ford Australia built the first ute, released in 1934, after a farmer's wife asked for a car to drive to church and take the _____ to market.
The Granny Smith apple was first grown in Sydney by _____.
The Dingo Fence, one of the longest fences in the world, was built to protect _____.
From 1 January 2021 the national anthem's line "For we are young and free" became "For we are _____ and free".
The last known thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, died in captivity in 1936 at a zoo in _____.
In 1894 South Australia passed a law making it the first place in the world to let women stand for _____.
Qantas began in outback Queensland in 1920, and its name stands for Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial _____.
Holden, the old Aussie car brand, started in Adelaide in 1856 as a maker of horse _____.
On election day, a sausage in bread bought from the barbecue at a polling place is nicknamed a _____ sausage.
Cane toads were brought to Queensland in 1935 from _____ to fight beetles in the sugar cane.
The shell-shaped roof of the Sydney Opera House is covered in more than a million tiles made in _____.
The rules of Australian Rules football were first written down in Melbourne in 1859, partly to keep _____ fit over winter.
The Melbourne Cup is run on the first _____ of November.
The Sydney Harbour Bridge is nicknamed the _____.
